implementation_notes: System.Threading.Monitor is the .NET intrinsic monitor: lock is shorthand for Enter/Exit, and Monitor.Wait releases the lock, parks the thread in the object's wait queue and re-acquires before returning, while Pulse/PulseAll must be called from inside the synchronized block and a pulse with no waiter is simply lost. The guard is therefore the same predicate loop as in Java - the docs describe the ready queue and wait queue explicitly - and the classic form remains the right choice for synchronous, thread-affine code. For server code that must not block a thread-pool thread, the same suspension is expressed by SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync or System.Threading.Channels, where the wait is a Task instead of a parked thread.
pitfalls: Monitor.Wait must sit in a loop: it returns after any Pulse on the same object, not because this thread's predicate became true.
Using one lock object for unrelated guards lets a Pulse wake the wrong waiter class and leaves the intended one blocked.
Awaiting inside a lock (or blocking on a Task.Result inside it) deadlocks the wait set; keep asynchronous waits and monitor waits on separate paths.

variants.name: SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync / Channels (awaitable guard)
variants.implementation_notes: SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync suspends the async method instead of a thread and accepts a timeout and a CancellationToken, which is the modern shape of the same guard whenever the waiting side is asynchronous; the permit count is the predicate, and System.Threading.Channels adds a real queue when the guard is 'an item is available'. Pair every successful WaitAsync with exactly one Release (or use a channel), and keep the classic Monitor form for synchronous code where the guard and the state mutation must happen under one lock.
pitfalls: A missing Release on an exception path permanently shrinks the permit count until the guard never opens again.
Mixing Monitor.Wait (thread-affine) and SemaphoreSlim waits over the same state reintroduces the races the guard was meant to remove.
